analysis.one_liner: Makes utilities, their executives, and their lobbyists repay customers overcharged through corruption.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 15, 2026 by Rep. Marcy Kaptur with one cosponsor, and referred to six House committees, where it has received no action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a federal fund to repay households and businesses that paid inflated utility rates caused by corruption, such as bribery of officials or manipulated rate filings. The money would be collected from the utilities involved, their top executives, and their lobbyists, after a court, settlement, or regulatory order establishes liability. Payments would go to ratepayers, state consumer advocate offices that helped prove the misconduct, and community restoration grants, with a public database tracking every collection and payout. It also mandates prison for utility executives, lobbyists, or officials convicted of bribery or related crimes.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that were customers of a utility found to have engaged in covered corruption would claim refunds for what they overpaid, prioritizing residential customers. Communities where at least 60 percent of residents were customers of the offending utility would get restoration grants for infrastructure, clean energy, broadband, and environmental cleanup, and state consumer advocate offices would be reimbursed for litigation that helped expose the misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Utility customers overcharged by corrupt utilities

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Ratepayer Justice Fund to send direct relief payments to eligible ratepayers as a refundable tax credit, or a direct payment for those who don't file tax returns, with residential customers prioritized [S2].

Funds the restitution by assessing covered utilities, C-suite executives, and their lobbyists for ratepayer costs of criminal mismanagement and their unjust enrichment, including executive bonuses and equity attributable to corruptly obtained rate approvals [S2].

Reimburses state consumer advocate offices for verified investigation and litigation expenses that materially helped establish the misconduct, and bars passing those reimbursement costs on to ratepayers [S2].

Provides community restoration grants of up to 5 percent of the fund, with no matching requirement, for infrastructure, clean energy, small business development, broadband, and environmental remediation in designated communities [S2].

Requires mandatory prison terms for public officials, C-suite executives, or lobbyists convicted of public corruption, honest services fraud, wire fraud, racketeering conspiracy, or bribery tied to a covered utility [S2].
Requires a public, searchable database of every assessment, collection, enforcement action, and grant, plus annual reports to Congress and audits of claims by the Treasury Inspector General [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Investor-owned electric and gas utilities and their corporate parents, their chief executives and other top officers, and their lobbyists would be assessed for overcharges, profits, and compensation attributable to the misconduct, and could face liens or garnishment if they do not pay. Utilities would also have to hand over customer records to verify claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Utilities, their executives, and their lobbyists

drawbacks.text: Funding depends entirely on what can actually be collected from utilities and individuals, so relief payments could be delayed, reduced, or unavailable if the liable parties are insolvent or contest the assessments [S2].

The bill prohibits passing consumer advocate reimbursement costs to ratepayers but does not generally bar utilities from recovering their own assessment costs through future rate cases, which could shift part of the bill onto the very customers it is meant to compensate [S2].

Mandatory imprisonment for 'any term of years' for officials, executives, and lobbyists convicted of specified offenses removes judicial sentencing discretion that critics of mandatory minimums typically defend [S2].

A federal restitution layer on top of state ratemaking creates complexity: the bill directs conflicting federal and state determinations to be resolved in favor of whichever produces the highest relief payment, which could lengthen litigation and invite disputes with state regulators [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and specific harm: customers who paid rates inflated by corruption and communities left with neglected infrastructure. Its protections against double recovery, its audits, and its use of existing state records are responsible design features. The main risks are practical, not conceptual: recovery is only as good as the collections, federal-state overlap could slow payouts, and the bill does not stop utilities from recouping their own assessments through future rates. As a bill addressing corruption directly affecting household bills, its benefits to ordinary people would likely outweigh its costs if it worked as written.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2026 and referred to six House committees, and no committee has taken it up, so it has never come to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the Ratepayer Justice and Commercial Power Accountability Act in the House on July 15, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to six committees: Energy and Commerce, plus Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Small Business, Financial Services, and Agriculture [S4].
Kaptur delivered introductory remarks on the measure on July 16, 2026 [S4].
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no committee has scheduled a hearing or markup and no vote has occurred [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: It is too early to name winners: the bill has only been referred to committees, so utilities and their executives currently face no new liability and ratepayers have received nothing new. If it stalls, the beneficiaries of inaction would be the utilities, executives, and lobbyists the bill would assess.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support is from two House Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor); no Republican has signed on and no recorded vote or stated opposition exists yet.

industries.note: They would be assessed for ratepayer losses and unjust enrichment from misconduct, plus prejudgment interest, and could face liens or garnishment; their customer records would be subject to federal demands. Because the bill's mechanism is clawing back what customers overpaid, the industry's financial interest runs directly against ratepayers here.

Top executives and lobbyists would be personally assessed for bonuses, equity, and other gains tied to corruptly approved rates, and face mandatory prison if convicted of bribery or related crimes. This is the bill's most direct accountability provision.
They would be reimbursed from the fund for investigation and litigation expenses that helped establish utility misconduct, strengthening public-side representation in rate cases.

industries.industry: Construction, clean energy, and broadband sectors in affected communities
industries.note: Community restoration grants for infrastructure, clean energy, grid resilience, and broadband would flow to local governments and nonprofits in communities served by offending utilities, creating work for these sectors while repairing harm to residents.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, one cosponsor, no bipartisan support, and referral split across six committees, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or floor vote and would probably expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
